title: Florida Fights Drowning Risk for Autistic Kids with Specialized Swim Lessons
summary: For many kids with autism, water is sensory bliss—the sparkle, the pressure, the feel on their skin. But that attraction comes with a tragic statistic: they are 160 times more likely to die from drowning than their peers, according to a 2017 Columbia University study. In Florida, a state dotted with pools, lakes, and beaches, the risk is especially acute. Five-year-old Mackenzie Wesley adores the water. Her mom, Brittany Bucknor, is acutely aware of the danger. "In Florida, there's water everywhere, and with kids on the spectrum, it's a way higher rate of having an incident of drowning," she says. About half of autistic children have a tendency to wander from safe settings, and when they encounter water, the combination can be deadly. Florida is fighting back. A new law requires healthcare providers to give parents of newborns information on drowning prevention and a state swim program. The voucher, about $200, covers up to eight lessons. Mackenzie's family found the YMCA of South Florida's Swim Buddies program, which serves over 600 children with disabilities—more than 60% of them with autism. The program's hallmark is individualization. Instructors assess each child and tailor lessons, using colorful toys for positive reinforcement. "We come at everything with a whole-person approach—the physical, the emotional, the social," says Garland Jones, the senior program director. Researchers Tania Santiago Perez and Tana Carson from Florida International University have studied the program and found that kids can improve swim skills in just five or six sessions. Each lesson starts with group introductions to build trust and social skills. Because many autistic children are prone to "eloping," or suddenly running away, instructors stay within arm's reach. During one session, a child dashed out of the pool, and the therapist gently but firmly guided him back. The program is overwhelmed with requests, and Jones hopes for more state funding. But for families like Mackenzie's, it's a lifeline. "These tragedies are so preventable," Bucknor says, "but if a child doesn't have access to drowning prevention, those statistics will only continue."
why_it_matters: This story reveals how a targeted public policy can confront a life-threatening inequality. For middle schoolers, it underscores that even small programs—like eight swim lessons—can dramatically reduce deaths and shows how science, empathy, and law can combine to protect vulnerable communities.

keywords.explanation: Sensory refers to how something feels to the senses, like the sparkle and touch of water that many autistic children find calming or enjoyable.
Eloping is a term used in the autism community for when a person suddenly runs away from a safe space, which can put them in danger near water.
Individualization means tailoring lessons to each child's unique abilities and needs, rather than using the same method for everyone.
Acutely means very sharply or intensely; a mom who is acutely aware of danger feels the risk deeply and constantly.
Hallmark is a distinguishing feature or typical quality—here, the Swim Buddies program’s main characteristic is its personal approach.
A lifeline is something that provides crucial support or rescue, like the swim program that can literally save lives for families.

background_read: Drowning is the leading cause of death for children with autism, and about half of autistic children have a tendency to wander or 'elope' from safe places. A landmark 2017 study by Columbia University (a research university in New York) quantified the risk as 160 times higher than for other kids, drawing national attention to the issue.

Florida has one of the highest drowning rates in the U.S. due to its thousands of residential pools, canals, and beaches. The state had already funded some water-safety programs, but the new law mandating that hospitals share prevention info is a more direct response to the autism-specific danger.

The YMCA of South Florida's Swim Buddies program is part of a broader YMCA (Young Men's Christian Association, a nonprofit that runs community programs) push to include people with disabilities. Researchers at Florida International University (FIU, a public university in Miami) have been studying its methods to see if short-term adaptive lessons can really save lives.

perspectives.description: Families see the program as literally saving their children's lives. Knowing that wandering and water are a deadly mix, they support any measure that gives their kids a better chance. The voucher system removes a financial barrier, and the individual attention builds trust—something many parents feel is missing in typical lessons.

Even though the program is effective, it is 'overwhelmed with requests' and cannot serve every child who needs it. Critics argue that $200 for eight lessons is not enough for long-term safety, and that relying on a single nonprofit like the YMCA leaves huge gaps. Without more state funding, many families will remain unprotected.

Academics point to the data: a 160-times higher risk is a clear public health crisis. They see programs like Swim Buddies as evidence-based interventions that should be scaled up, but also stress that drownings are part of a larger pattern of safety risks for autistic individuals. Research is needed to see if five or six sessions are enough for lasting water competence.

Looking ahead, some experts call for mandatory water-safety education in schools, more lifeguards trained in autism, and technology like tracking devices for children who wander. The new Florida law could become a model for other states, but only if follow-up studies prove that access to prevention truly lowers the death toll. The hope is that next year, the program's waiting list will shrink instead of growing.
